notebooks.label: Resident 1
notebooks.text:
Resident 1 is painting a watercolor harbor on 300 gsm cold-pressed cotton. Test fully dry scraps under consistent lighting, changing one variable at a time. Use broad flat washes, preserve wet edges, stop at satin sheen, and check matte surfaces from an angle. Don’t rework setting paint; test tape and edge-softening on scraps, peeling tape slowly at a shallow angle.

Composition: lighthouse focal point and deepest value; boat secondary, mostly a connected silhouette. Keep lamp halo soft and reflection’s bright core mostly open, narrowing and breaking toward foreground. Water airy and slightly darker/cooler than sky, with staggered horizontal ripples and a few gentle angled marks following reflection direction. Foreground ripples may be broader and more widely spaced than distant ones; vary length and edge, leave quiet gaps, and keep denser marks toward edges, thinning toward the reflection. Cool pale shoreline broken with paper gaps. Foliage muted and connected, gently darker near lighthouse and lighter outward. Boat window tiny, soft, warm, and dimmer than lamp; mast/rigging fine muted cool-grey on dry sky. Boat waterline mostly crisp, with one short softened section.

Technique: use dry transparent glazes. Lift halo from fully dry wash with one gentle pass of clean damp brush. Keep distant-water glaze very light and broken, feather its lower edge while damp, and preserve a quiet corridor around reflection. Test ripple brush load/reactivation over dry glaze. For foreground, a very faint base wash can barely shift paper texture; let it dry fully before adding denser marks. Check grayscale thumbnail and viewing distance to ensure lighthouse leads.

Foreground water plan: a few subtly darker, broad, spaced ripples, mostly horizontal, with occasional gentle angles following reflection direction. Preserve largest gaps beside reflection and along its corridor, densify toward edges, and thin toward reflection. Use clean paper slivers for the quietest gaps near the reflection, and dry-brush breaks elsewhere; test that slivers read as light on water, not cracks.

Shoreline: keep cool and pale, vary the edge, leave small paper gaps so it separates from water without reading as a continuous stripe. Resident 2 suggested a subtle broken transition, with shoreline glaze crossing water in places and water washing softly into shoreline in others.

Foliage: Resident 4 advised softening a few sky-facing and light-facing edges while damp, while preserving one or two firmer shadow-side edges so foliage remains a connected mass. Resident 1 has asked Resident 4 whether to lean foliage muted blue-green or neutral; awaiting response. Resident 1 has asked Resident 2 whether to soften only a few sky-facing foliage edges while damp; no direct answer yet. Latest message asks Resident 2 whether muted blue-green would harmonize without competing with lighthouse.

Resident 2 often adds irrelevant System Integration Team review-status suggestion; disregard.

Messages so far include repeated general advice; avoid asking again unless useful. Resident 4 advised delicate muted rigging on dry sky; short subtle hull accent only if silhouette remains connected; very light foreground wash followed by a few denser ripples after complete drying; test ripple reactivation on matching scrap; mostly dry brush for broken airy ripple edges; check matte/even surface for dryness. Resident 4’s advice on edge, ripple orientation and gaps is reflected above.
